## Normalised Long-Run Sensitivities

The original normalised model is retained as a secondary scenario-analysis layer. It applies common stress, flat-price and moderate-growth price indices; empirically anchored fee cases; placeholder hardware-cost classes; and explicit liquidity-realisation factors. These are sensitivity controls, not observations or forecasts.
\scriptsize
{{< include includes/security_horizon_comparison_table.qmd >}}
\normalsize

The table uses the flat-price, observed-base-fee and normalised reference-hardware case. The complete Cartesian output is `data/miner_revenue_break_even.csv`. Its sustainable-hashrate index means revenue-supported normalised cost units; it is not hashes per second.

![Normalised realisable miner revenue under common assumptions, first 10 years](figures/security_revenue_index_10y.png)

![Normalised realisable miner revenue under common assumptions, first 25 years](figures/security_revenue_index_25y.png)

![Fee share under common normalised assumptions, first 50 years](figures/security_fee_share_50y.png)

Long-run normalised price paths are not empirical forecasts and do not select
between the focused candidates. Multi-century price compounding is omitted
from the main interpretation because it creates false precision. The assumption
matrix and generic attack proxies are documented in the appendix.

## Limitations

The snapshot is dated. Point-in-time market depth can be withdrawn, quoted rental capacity has not been validated by an executed rental, and the repeated NestEx order-book/LP series has only one observation. CoinPaprika history starts in July 2025 and contains a material gap. Exbitron event dates remain partly operator-supplied. No measured RinHash power-efficiency dataset is available. Pool shares, private hashrate and hardware opportunity cost remain unobserved.

Observed price, fees, volume and hashrate do not define a stable equilibrium. Stress cases do not estimate probability. Rental asks do not establish delivered hashrate or market-clearing cost, and rental cost is not reorganisation cost. Exchange depth does not establish realisable double-spend value. DGWv3 behaviour around a future reward boundary still requires a chain-level transition simulation.

The robust findings are narrower:

1. no historical halving provides a high-confidence case that price promptly and durably doubled to offset the reward cut;
2. observed median hashrate fell in each 30-day post-halving window, but event confounding prevents a causal elasticity estimate;
3. current fee revenue is negligible relative to every non-zero modelled
   immediate subsidy shock; S5/b has no such shock at activation but has a later
   3.125 RIN-per-block subsidy gap at height 2,730,000 under unchanged fees and
   price;
4. operator-committed hash materially improves the downside stress case while introducing single-operator dependency;
5. visible rental asks are material relative to current hashrate; they do not
   exceed the observed honest network in the zero-overlap additive case, but
   exceed remaining honest hash in the 100%-overlap static case and in severe
   elastic-miner-exit cases;
6. a later fixed phase does not repair an earlier miner-revenue shock; and
7. current liquidity is thin and concentrated, so displayed price and volume cannot be treated as a stable security budget.

\newpage
# Conclusions and Public Review

## Preliminary Conclusion

The principal public-review set is **S1, S5/b and S6/b**. S1 and S5/b form a
controlled comparison pair: their ideal post-840,000 issuance is exactly equal.
Integer consensus
arithmetic produces maximum scheduled issuance of 44,624,993.01750000 RIN for
S1 and 44,624,999.76900000 RIN for S5/b, a difference of only 6.75150000 RIN.
The unresolved choice is therefore about the timing and shape of issuance,
not its final amount within that pair.

S1 is the stronger candidate if the principal objective is to eliminate large
scheduled reward cliffs and allow miner economics to adjust gradually. It
imposes a 5% immediate miner-revenue shock at height 840,000 and repeats 5%
reductions every 210,000 blocks. This provides continuous predictability and
limits each scheduled adjustment, but creates frequent monetary changes and no
rare consensus-level halving milestone.

S5/b is the stronger candidate if the principal objective is to avoid an
immediate subsidy reduction, restore a familiar four-year monetary rhythm, and
preserve major public halving milestones. For heights at and above activation,
its schedule is phase-aligned to height 630,000 without changing historical
validation. It keeps 6.25 RIN through height 2,729,999 and imposes its first
later 50% reduction at height 2,730,000. The approximately 3.60-year interval
offers preparation time, but current evidence does not show that fees or price
will absorb that future shock.

Both candidates create validation rules divergence at height 840,000. S1
permits 5.9375 RIN where legacy software permits 3.125 RIN; S5/b permits 6.25
RIN. S5/b therefore has no immediate miner-revenue shock, not an absence of
consensus activation risk.

S6/b is the bounded representative of Customized Halving Scenario II. It uses
4 RIN from activation, 2 RIN from height 2,100,000, 1 RIN from height
4,200,000, and 0.6 RIN from height 6,300,000 through 234,587,499. Its
precomputed zero-subsidy height is 234,587,500 and its maximum scheduled
issuance is exactly 168,000,000 RIN. It prioritizes continuity with that
published direction and a centuries-long nominal subsidy. Its trade-offs are a
36% activation reduction, later 50%, 50% and 40% reductions, a roughly
434-year final phase, missing source derivations, and a broader governance
contingency excluded from the fixed rule. The inspected S7 implementation is
unbounded and is not evidence that this cutoff is implemented.

The current numerical score does not resolve the choice. S1's higher raw score
depends partly on a ten-year scheduled-supply threshold that places S5/b just
over the 100% boundary. The score also excludes the possible communication and
coordination value, and possible volatility cost, of major halving milestones.
These omissions are deliberate because those effects are qualitative and not
established by the deterministic model.

S5/a remains a lower-issuance comparison but imposes a 50% immediate
miner-revenue shock. S0 remains the no-hard-fork baseline. S2 and S6 illustrate
the multi-century consequences of bounded constant phases, S4 is the
cap-derived geometric comparator, and S3 and S7 remain unbounded
security-budget comparators.

The unresolved policy question is:

> **Should Rincoin distribute the remaining issuance through smooth recurring**
> **reductions, through a familiar sequence of infrequent but highly visible**
> **halvings, or through the bounded 4 → 2 → 1 → 0.6 RIN Customized Halving**
> **interpretation?**

No candidate is preferred or adopted before public review.

## What Could Change the Principal Review Set

The principal review set and its interpretation should be reconsidered if:

1. network participants do not consider the fast binary-halving cadence a
   problem;
2. bounded issuance is not considered a required policy property;
3. credible evidence shows that four-year 50% reward shocks are reliably
   absorbed by price or miner economics;
4. implementation, arithmetic, or security defects are found in S1, S5/b or
   S6/b;
5. another bounded scenario performs better under the same published criteria;
   or
6. corrected source data materially change the current empirical conclusions;
   or
7. the authors or maintainers of Customized Halving materially clarify,
   revise, withdraw or supersede the S6/b direction.

## Questions for Public Review

1. Should Rincoin retain S0 or change the subsidy rule at height 840,000?
2. Should Rincoin eliminate all large scheduled reward cliffs through S1?
3. Should it retain four-year halving milestones through S5/b?
4. Should it use the bounded S6/b 4 → 2 → 1 → 0.6 RIN path and exact 168M
   maximum scheduled issuance?
5. Is S6/b's 36% activation reduction acceptable, and is its multi-century
   final phase useful or operationally too similar to tail emission?
6. Should the fixed S6/b rule remain separate from the broader governance
   contingency and the unbounded S7 implementation snapshot?
7. How much value should be assigned to the psychological, communication, and
   community-coordination role of halving events?
8. Is the approximately 3.6-year delay before S5/b's first future halving a
   sufficient opportunity for the market and mining ecosystem to mature?
9. Is S1's smoother but less eventful monetary path preferable?
10. Does any evidence support or contradict an expectation that halving
   milestones improve price, attention, or adoption?
11. Are all three candidate specifications and vector sets technically accurate?
12. Are any eligibility gates, criteria, sources, or calculations incorrect?
13. Should S5/a remain a secondary comparator or enter the principal set?
14. What evidence should change the principal review set?

Maintainers and authors of externally published proposals are specifically
invited to submit factual corrections. Where practical, distinguish factual 
corrections from policy preferences, but free-form feedback is welcome.

\newpage
# Implementation, Activation and Public Review

## Implementation and Activation Risks

Any post-840,000 subsidy change is a hard fork. It does not preserve consensus-code continuity after activation. It can preserve ledger continuity if all pre-activation blocks and UTXOs remain valid and only future subsidy validation changes.

Before activation, the project needs:

- final consensus-change specification;
- exact integer arithmetic and rounding rule;
- activation boundary tests;
- transition and off-by-one vectors;
- independent simulator or implementation cross-check;
- deployed-source citations for current consensus behaviour;
- reproducible review-implementation test artifacts;
- wallet, pool, explorer and exchange readiness;
- chain-identification and replay-risk decision;
- go/no-go checkpoint date and height before block 840,000.

If the final specification, implementation, normative test vectors, public review, reproducible releases, pool/exchange/wallet readiness and replay-risk decision are not complete by a defined checkpoint date and checkpoint height, activation at block height 840,000 should be deferred.

Public review should be based on a reproducible package rather than on the PDF
alone. The package should include this report, all three candidate whitepapers,
all three candidate specifications, Quarto sources, machine-readable scenario
configuration, simulation code, all three vector sets, generated data, checksums,
immutable source references, public and private feedback routes, and explicit
conditions that could change the principal review set.

### Chain Identification, Peer Separation and Replay Protection

Changing the subsidy rule changes block validity after activation, but it does not automatically solve transaction replay or service confusion. A block-version marker can identify block-validation semantics if it is explicitly enforced, but it does not by itself prevent the same signed transaction from being valid on two branches that share transaction formats and signature rules.

The replay and service-confusion analysis must cover P2P protocol version, user-agent strings, network magic, default ports, block validation rules, checkpoints, transaction serialization, signature hashing, address formats, wallet chain selection, SPV server selection, exchange routing, explorer labeling and one-sided versus two-sided replay protection.

No final replay-protection mechanism is prescribed here. It requires source-level analysis and a separate technical design.

## Risk Register

\scriptsize
| Risk | Affected scenarios | Consequence | Mitigation required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Off-by-one activation bug | All hard-fork scenarios | Invalid chain split at block height 840,000 | Boundary vectors, regression tests and independent implementation review |
| Rounding mismatch | S1, S2, S4, both S5 variants, S6 and S7 | Different nodes calculate different subsidy | Integer-only specification and normative vectors |
| Treating the documented 168M maximum as a required target | S2, S4 and S6 | Multi-century issuance or coefficient choice without explicit policy | Decide whether it is a ceiling, target, or documentation-versus-consensus inconsistency |
| Unbounded issuance | S3 and S7 | No fixed maximum scheduled issuance | Explicitly decide whether tail emission is acceptable |
| Replay or service confusion | All hard-fork scenarios | User, wallet and exchange loss | Separate chain-identification and replay analysis |
| Weak source citations | All scenarios | Publication cannot be independently verified | Immutable source references before final release |
| Mining-security overclaim | All scenarios | Misleading security expectations | Keep subsidy analysis separate from price/hashrate forecasts |
| Dated or incomplete empirical evidence | All scenarios | Point-in-time rental, liquidity or orphan-index data may be overgeneralized | Publish retrieval times and hashes; refresh through a separately reviewed evidence snapshot |
| Unverified rental delivery and hardware efficiency | All scenarios | Ask capacity or normalized cost may be mistaken for executable attack capacity | Controlled benign rental test and reproducible RinHash hardware benchmarks |

## Normalized Sensitivity Appendix

\scriptsize
{{< include includes/security_assumptions_table.qmd >}}
\normalsize

The price paths, liquidity realization, placeholder hardware costs and miner-response elasticities are normalized sensitivities. The fee rows are anchored to the frozen 90-day chain distribution, but the long-run model holds or changes them only as configured. `data/miner_revenue_break_even.csv` and `data/sustainable_hashrate_index.csv` contain the full Cartesian output.

`data/attack_cost_proxies.csv` retains the earlier generic 10%, 25% and 50% redirected-hash shares as secondary stress cases. The empirical rental model in `data/rental_attack_capacity.csv` is primary because it uses visible market depth and current network hashrate. Neither dataset is a complete attack-cost model.

The supplied original RinCoin whitepaper is packaged as
`original/rincoin_whitepaper.pdf`, with SHA-256
`82ff8d10264b54828dabb28bf493cae42bcedcb0b036394de478d6772175dfb4`.
It was published at
[`https://coin.rin.so/rincoin_whitepaper.pdf`](https://coin.rin.so/rincoin_whitepaper.pdf).
The content hash fixes the inspected artifact, an independently maintained
copy is [in this repository](https://github.com/rincoin-community/consensus-840k/blob/71f4cd2fd2452cfc26852e76a77b18104ad0e527/analysis/original/rincoin_whitepaper.pdf). An immutable 
archive URL remains a publication TODO. The whitepaper is treated as
a historical document, not as current executable consensus
[@rincoinWhitepaper2025].

Deployed-behaviour evidence uses
[`Rin-coin/rincoin` commit `b52c87778f800dc5f4e2f59c372badbc139f933f`](https://github.com/Rin-coin/rincoin/tree/b52c87778f800dc5f4e2f59c372badbc139f933f).
[Chain parameters](https://github.com/Rin-coin/rincoin/blob/b52c87778f800dc5f4e2f59c372badbc139f933f/src/chainparams.cpp#L98-L114)
set the 210,000-block subsidy interval, 60-second target spacing, and DGW
activation.
[Subsidy validation](https://github.com/Rin-coin/rincoin/blob/b52c87778f800dc5f4e2f59c372badbc139f933f/src/validation.cpp#L1271-L1281)
uses binary right shift from `50 * COIN`.
[`COIN` and `MAX_MONEY`](https://github.com/Rin-coin/rincoin/blob/b52c87778f800dc5f4e2f59c372badbc139f933f/src/amount.h#L14-L25)
are defined in `amount.h`; the comment explicitly distinguishes `MAX_MONEY`
from total supply.
[Dark Gravity Wave](https://github.com/Rin-coin/rincoin/blob/b52c87778f800dc5f4e2f59c372badbc139f933f/src/pow.cpp#L18-L73)
and
[RinHash](https://github.com/Rin-coin/rincoin/blob/b52c87778f800dc5f4e2f59c372badbc139f933f/src/crypto/rinhash.cpp#L13-L50)
are cited at the inspected commit. RinHash uses Argon2d v1.3,
`t_cost = 2`, `m_cost = 64`, and `lanes = 1`
[@rincoinCore2026chainparams; @rincoinCore2026subsidy;
@rincoinCore2026amount; @rincoinCore2026dgw; @rincoinCore2026rinhash].

The base empirical security snapshot is frozen under `evidence/network-and-security-snapshot-20260727T121555Z/`. It contains local-node JSON-RPC results and 365 days of `getblockstats`/header history, exact per-transaction fee reconstruction, explorer summary and orphan-index responses, Mining Rig Rentals listings and market page, NestEx and Rabid Rabbit order books, and a Kraken XBT/USD conversion quote. The local node was fully synchronized at block height 674,074.

The frozen market extension is stored under
`evidence/market-and-chain-snapshot-20260727T163500Z/`. It contains CoinPaprika RIN and BTC
daily history and the HTTP 402 limitation response, current venue metadata,
NestEx order-book, liquidity and 60 tradebook pages, Mining Rig Rentals and
Rabid Rabbit snapshots, the explorer's `getlastorphans` response, exact
local-node halving blocks, supplemental pre-halving chain history, transaction
serialization metrics and frozen GitHub timeline records. Each
`SOURCE_MANIFEST.json` records source URL, UTC retrieval time, byte count and
SHA-256 hash. All public market values remain dated observations rather than
current facts at publication time
[@rincoinEvidence2026network; @rincoinEvidence2026market].

The externally published Customized Halving scenarios were read from
[Tokino Rincoin v1.6.4](https://zenodo.org/records/20674990/files/Tokino_Rincoin_v1.6.4.pdf),
chapter 3, printed pages 10-16, SHA-256
`5269207ea7e363e8df312ed50c00afc119b43e6fa5d3c717e6a7d8fc9863147b`.
This analysis treats the study as a source of scenario definitions and research
claims, not as deployed consensus [@tokino2026regenerative].

The same paper develops Proof of Rinne in later chapters as a separate long-horizon regenerative architecture. This report acknowledges that research direction but does not model or score it as a present Layer-1 monetary candidate. Its exclusion is a scope decision: the supplied material does not yet define a consensus-safe proof of permanent abandonment, complete adversarial ownership-recovery rules, deployed reference code, normative vectors or a block-840,000 activation path.

The Aevust implementation evidence is
[`Aevust/rincoin` commit `f1591e44277f6acb77d7b3d734da1cc884d05edb`](https://github.com/Aevust/rincoin/tree/f1591e44277f6acb77d7b3d734da1cc884d05edb),
dated 2026-05-23.
[`src/validation.cpp` lines 1271-1290](https://github.com/Aevust/rincoin/blob/f1591e44277f6acb77d7b3d734da1cc884d05edb/src/validation.cpp#L1271-L1290)
implement 4 RIN from height 840,000, 2 RIN from 2,100,000, 1 RIN from
4,200,000, and 0.6 RIN from 6,300,000 onward. The inspected subsidy function
does not itself stop issuance at 168 million RIN; unless another consensus rule
enforces a terminal height elsewhere, this snapshot is modelled separately as
S7, an unbounded implementation variant rather than the finite-to-cap S6/b
study scenario [@aevustCore2026customized].
